contract.note: Plain reading (S&P 500 price return from the 2024 close, at a common publication-time cutoff) is ordinary and fair. The result depends on the unstated quote timestamp.

evidence.note: AP report of the April 10 close: S&P 500 down 10.4% for the year. Its cutoff is after the post (17:15Z ≈ 1:15 p.m. ET), so it cannot test the quoted pair.

Motley Fool: NVDA down about 21% YTD around 1 p.m. ET. A rounded intraday figure with no S&P YTD figure at the same time, so it cannot settle 23.4% vs 11.5%. Directionally consistent with Nvidia falling much more.

reviews.rationale: The packet has no pair of NVIDIA and S&P 500 YTD figures at a common cutoff matching the post. The 10.4% close and the ~21% intraday NVDA figure use different, later or rounded cutoffs, so they neither confirm nor refute the quoted percentages. Both suggest Nvidia was down much more than the index, but the precise claim is not settled.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his April 10, 2025 post.

semantics.note: Faithful: marketing premise plus a causal claim that persistent reliability problems limit practical use.

contract.note: Plain reading (prominent suppliers' AGI messaging; errors limiting some important uses, not all) is ordinary and fair. Period Jan 1–Apr 10, 2025 is reasonable.

evidence.note: Altman, Jan 2025: confident OpenAI knows how to build AGI. Primary evidence of the near-AGI pitch itself.
METR independent evaluation, Mar 2025: agents cannot reliably handle even low-skill computer work; struggle with long action sequences. Links unreliability to practical limits.
OpenAI deep research launch, Feb 2025: admits hallucinations and poor calibration, which limit reliance on its reports. A company disclosure against its own interest.
GPT-4.5, Feb 2025: expects fewer hallucinations. Shows improvement, not the removal of practical limits. Snapshot is later, but the quoted text is from Feb 2025.

reviews.rationale: Supplier messaging in the period promoted near-term AGI (e1). An independent evaluation (e2) and the supplier's own product limitations (e3) tie persistent errors to concrete limits on useful work. e4 shows expected improvement but does not show the constraints were gone. Both parts of the claim hold under the plain reading.
